lesson.title: Proving Who Sent It and That It Wasn't Touched
lesson.summary: A digital signature combines a hash function with public key cryptography so a signer can prove both their identity and that a message has not been altered, signing with their private key while letting anyone verify with the corresponding public key.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters introduced the two ingredients a digital signature combines. Public key cryptography gives every party a private key that only they hold and a public key that anyone can check against. Hash functions turn any message, of any length, into a fixed size fingerprint that changes completely if even one bit of the input changes. A digital signature puts these together to solve a problem neither one solves alone: proving that a specific message really came from a specific sender and was not altered along the way.

The process works like this. The signer first hashes the message they want to sign, producing a fixed size digest. They then run a signing algorithm over that digest using their private key, producing the signature itself, which gets attached to or sent alongside the original message. Anyone who wants to verify the signature recomputes the hash of the message they received, then uses the signer's public key to check whether the attached signature is valid for that particular digest. If the check passes, the verifier has two guarantees at once. The first is authenticity: only someone holding the matching private key could have produced a signature that checks out correctly against the corresponding public key. The second is integrity: if even a single bit of the message had changed between signing and verification, the recomputed hash would not match the one the signature was actually made over, and verification would fail.

In RSA specifically, the signing operation is literally the same mathematical operation as RSA decryption, just applied to a hash instead of a ciphertext, which is why people sometimes describe RSA signing informally as encrypting the hash with the private key. That description is accurate for RSA, but it is not universally true of every signature scheme. ECDSA, another widely used signature algorithm built on elliptic curve cryptography, uses a distinct signing algorithm that is not simply encryption run in reverse. Regardless of which specific algorithm is used underneath, every digital signature scheme provides the same two guarantees: authenticity and integrity.

It is worth being precise about what a signature does not provide. A signed message is not automatically a secret message. Signing proves who sent something and that it has not been changed, but it says nothing about whether anyone else can read it, that is a separate property, confidentiality, provided by encryption if it is needed at all. A contract can be publicly readable and still meaningfully signed.

This exact sign with the private key, verify with the public key pattern reappears constantly in the rest of this unit. It is what lets a certificate authority vouch for someone's public key by signing a certificate, covered two chapters from now, and it is what lets DNSSEC, covered next, make a DNS response provably genuine rather than just plausible.
